sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Our Luxembourg data is recent, so there is no city trend yet; the figures below are for weekdays and weekends in August and September 2026.

Luxembourg's main policy for reducing car use has been public transport. Since March 2020 public transport has been free of charge nationwide, with first-class rail the exception, which the government describes as aimed at cutting road traffic [0]. Tram ridership rose from 6.2 million in 2019 to 31.7 million in 2024, as the network grew, and rail from 25 to 31.3 million [1]. The tram was reported to be carrying about 100,000 passengers a day in April 2024 [2]. The city's mobility plan, presented in April 2024, aims for 51% of trips by public transport and soft mobility by 2035 and to hold motorised trips at their 2020 level, and says the parking situation needs reassessing or even overhauling [3].

Parking prices are moderate. On the street, the colour-coded zones range from €0.50 to €2 an hour [5], and a resident's first permit is free, with €60 for a second and €120 for a third [6]. For long stays the Gernsback car park on the Kirchberg raised its flat rate from €5 to €15 in February 2022; the mayor's reply noted that the city's park-and-ride sites are free for 24 hours [4]. Commuting across the border is shaped by tax rules: a France–Luxembourg agreement signed in 2022 raised the tax-free teleworking limit for French residents from 24 to 34 days from 2023 [15].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The city has been renewing its central car parks. The Royal-Hamilius garage, with 628 spaces and run by APCOA, was reported ready for its first customers in September 2018 [10]. The city announced that the Knuedler car park next to the city hall would reopen in phases from 28 November 2022 after renovation and extension, with a target of 749 spaces [7]. On the Kirchberg plateau the 595-space Gernsback car park opened in 2021 with 16 charging stations [9]. The largest addition is on the edge: the Stade de Luxembourg park-and-ride, a six-level car park with 1,993 spaces, opened in October 2023, free for the first 24 hours [8].

Technology is spreading from the car park to the street. The Indigo Neo app, available since June 2023, pays for parking by phone, covering about 35,000 spaces [11], and lets drivers enter the Fort Neipperg car park without a ticket by plate recognition [12]. The city publishes the free spaces of its car parks as open data [14] and has a dynamic guidance system. When it closed the Glacis car park in stages from June 2024 for summer events, it sent motorists to that system and to the largely free park-and-ride sites [13].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
All 17 car parks we measure come from the city's own parking data, and their prices are nearly uniform: €2 an hour in the centre, €2.40 and a €38 day ticket at Royal-Hamilius, €1 at two garages at the edge and a free park-and-ride. Price therefore says little about use. The 17 car parks average 40% on weekdays and 23% at weekends, a large weekday-weekend gap compared with most cities in our set.

The centre is steadily used, in the evening and at weekends too: Théâtre (62%, 64% at weekends), Knuedler (52%, 60%) and Saint-Esprit (38%, 42%). The fullest large car park is the €1 garage at the Rond Point Schuman (65% on weekdays). Further out some stand almost empty: Trois Glands (13%) and the €1 'Stade' garage (3%). The park-and-ride sites behave as commuter car parks. Bouillon (2,422 spaces) and the stadium site (1,824 spaces) are 43% and 41% occupied on weekdays and fall to 14% and 4% at weekends.
